source.title: Steering Vision-Language Models with Joint Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Huizhen Shu; Xuying Li; Hongxu Lin; Wenjie Sun; Hui Li

record.tranche_reason: The study applies sparse autoencoders and intervention tests to vision-language models, extending evidence about recoverable sparse features to a multimodal setting. It does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's SAE sparsity and reconstruction measurements and the reported feature-based interventions, including separately reported layer, category, architecture, and comparator results. Layer-selection scores and quoted results from prior work are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It trains Joint SAEs on mean-pooled vision/caption activations of three VLMs, then reports how well its decoder directions steer captions compared with baselines. L0 sparsity is imposed by the L1 objective, not discovered. Features are post-hoc clustered macro-concepts. Steering success is deliberately induced and measures the method's utility. The study never asks whether the models store more features than dimensions, or whether neurons spread features, so it does not test V4 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also stress that probe-optimal Layer 13 differs from steering-optimal Layer 25, so probe accuracy does not predict steerability. They also report that suppression stays flat across depths, with a caution against over-reading its magnitude.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sequence-pooled, paired vision/text Joint Sparse Autoencoders with a cosine alignment penalty and cross-modal activation interventions, rather than the Toy Models of Superposition setup or its toy-network geometry tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effectiveness varies with layer, semantic category, architecture, and dataset; the study reports Layer 25 as strongest in its LLaVA layer sweep and weaker effects near Layer 30.

fits_no_version.finding: Text-side decoder directions of an alignment-constrained SAE steer VLM captions toward target concepts. Success peaks at LLaVA Layer 25 (0.798) and drops at Layer 30 (0.152). An unaligned SAE with matched sparsity steers at 0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steerability of SAE feature directions in VLMs depends on layer and on cross-modal alignment of the dictionary.

record.problems: The authors state that generalization coverage is limited, additional architectures are tested at only one selected layer each, feature discovery uses global mean-pooling and post-hoc clustering, and some category/domain transfer is weaker. Suppression scores lack an unintervened or random-direction reference, so their absolute magnitude is cautioned against.
record.rows_left_out: No additional independently reported numeric feature-steering, sparsity, or reconstruction results bearing on V4 were left out.

untested.parts: No toy models, feature/dimension sweep, sparsity transition or geometry.
Capacity competition and importance-based allocation not examined.
Alternative origins of polysemanticity not examined.
No measure of features spread across neurons; SAE recovery is assumed and applied to sequence-pooled macro-level activations, not tested as evidence of sparse features.
Completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features not tested; features are re-aggregated by clustering.
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Suppression results: scores 5.04–5.78 across layers, no significant pairwise differences, and no unintervened reference.
ActAdd and VL-SAE per-category breakdowns (e.g., ActAdd 0.125 on Wild animal).

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Toy Models of Superposition only as motivation for SAEs. Its features are image/caption-level macro-concepts from mean-pooled activations, which the authors say are not token-level monosemantic units. The reader's V4 labels have been removed because the rows measure the method's steering utility, not the claim.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-versus-dimension sweep, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometric arrangements are tested.
The study does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from competition for limited representational capacity or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The study does not test whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure, or whether it is evidence for superposition.

The study tests sparse feature recovery and intervention utility in three VLMs; it does not establish how common such features are across LLMs generally or measure feature distribution across neurons in ordinary language-only LLMs.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features are not tested.
The study uses decoder directions and aggregates features into macro-concepts, but does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional feature representations.

relation.reason: Superposition motivates the SAE method; the measured outcomes concern deliberately injected steering directions and method comparisons.

tranche.reason: The study uses sparse dictionaries to develop and evaluate cross-modal steering. Its intervention-performance results do not test the catalog's superposition claim versions.

source_check.notes: The statement's 0% refers to standard VL-SAE; the unaligned JSAE ablation instead achieves 4.1%. Table 5's additive mean differences are not consistently compatible with Table 1's reported means; the checked row values are corroborated by Table 2.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: JSAE interventions at LLaVA Layers 13 and 25 and the selected layers of Qwen3-VL and Llama3-LLaVA
reader_labels.reason: Sparse JSAE features were used as intervention directions with substantial reported success in these settings (R02, R03, R05, R06, R10–R15, R19–R23).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Layer 7 and Layer 30; weaker categories and Flickr30k transfer; non-aligned SAE comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Steering strength varies by layer and category, some settings show little or no success, and the study tests only selected VLMs and layers (R01, R04, R16–R18, R21, R24–R27, R30, R32).
